questions.q: What are the four Yamanaka factors used to generate induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), and which one is an oncogene that poses a tumorigenicity risk in clinical applications?
questions.a: The four Yamanaka factors are Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, and c-Myc (OSKM). c-Myc is a proto-oncogene; its overexpression increases reprogramming efficiency but raises tumorigenicity risk, so later protocols often omit it (using OSK only) or use non-integrating methods. A wrong answer (e.g., listing Nanog instead of Klf4, or missing c-Myc) reveals the student memorised the acronym without understanding each factor's functional role and safety implication.

questions.q: A student claims: "iPSCs are exactly identical to embryonic stem cells because both are pluripotent." Explain why this statement is incorrect by comparing their origin, epigenetic status, and immunological compatibility for autologous therapy.
questions.a: iPSCs are *similar* but not *identical* to ESCs. Origin: ESCs come from the inner cell mass of a blastocyst; iPSCs are derived from somatic cells (e.g., skin fibroblasts) by reprogramming. Epigenetics: iPSCs may retain "epigenetic memory" of the donor somatic cell lineage, biasing differentiation. Immunology: Autologous iPSCs (from the patient's own cells) avoid immune rejection, whereas allogeneic ESCs require immunosuppression. A wrong answer that equates them entirely shows the student confuses functional potency (pluripotency) with molecular and clinical equivalence.

questions.q: A researcher reprograms human dermal fibroblasts using a lentiviral vector expressing OSKM. After 21 days, colonies appear. List the *minimum three validation assays* (with one molecular, one functional, and one in vivo test) that must be performed to confirm these colonies are bona fide iPSCs, and state the expected result for each.
questions.a: 1. Molecular: Immunostaining/qPCR for pluripotency markers (Oct4, Nanog, SSEA-4, TRA-1-60) — expected: positive expression. 2. Functional: In vitro embryoid body (EB) formation showing differentiation into all three germ layers (e.g., β-III-tubulin for ectoderm, α-SMA for mesoderm, AFP for endoderm) — expected: positive for all three. 3. In vivo: Teratoma assay in immunodeficient mice — expected: teratoma containing tissues from ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm. Missing any one assay (e.g., skipping teratoma) indicates incomplete validation understanding.

questions.q: Compare the reprogramming efficiency and genomic integration risk of the following delivery methods for Yamanaka factors: (a) integrating retrovirus/lentivirus, (b) non-integrating Sendai virus, (c) episomal plasmids, (d) mRNA transfection. Rank them from highest to lowest efficiency, and from highest to lowest integration risk. Explain the trade-off.
questions.a: Efficiency rank (high → low): (a) integrating virus > (b) Sendai virus > (c) episomal plasmids > (d) mRNA. Integration risk rank (high → low): (a) integrating virus > (b) Sendai virus (RNA virus, no DNA integration but persistent) > (c) episomal plasmids (rare integration) > (d) mRNA (zero integration). Trade-off: Higher efficiency methods (integrating viruses) leave permanent genetic modifications, risking insertional mutagenesis; clinical-grade iPSCs require footprint-free methods (mRNA, episomes) despite lower efficiency and higher technical difficulty. A student ranking mRNA as highest efficiency reveals confusion between *efficiency* and *safety*.

questions.q: Evaluate this claim: "Since iPSCs can be made from a patient's own cells, they completely solve the immune rejection problem in regenerative medicine." Defend or refute with three specific immunological or genetic arguments.
questions.a: Refute. Three arguments: (1) *Aberrant gene expression*: Reprogramming and culture can cause mutations, copy number variations, or epigenetic aberrations creating neoantigens. (2) *Mitochondrial DNA mismatch*: If donor mitochondria differ (e.g., in heteroplasmic patients), immune recognition may occur. (3) *Differentiation-derived immunogenicity*: Terminally differentiated cells from iPSCs may express minor histocompatibility antigens not present in the original somatic cell. A student accepting the claim uncritically ignores post-reprogramming genomic instability and the difference between *source* compatibility and *product* compatibility.

questions.q: Design a stepwise experimental workflow to generate clinical-grade, integration-free iPSCs from a 10 mL peripheral blood sample of a Type 1 diabetes patient, differentiate them into pancreatic β-like cells, and validate function *in vitro*. Specify the cell type targeted, reprogramming method, two key validation checkpoints, and one functional assay for β-cell maturity.
questions.a: Workflow: (1) Isolate PBMCs (CD34+ erythroblasts or T-cells) from blood. (2) Reprogram using episomal plasmids (pEB-C5: Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, L-Myc, Lin28; pEB-Tg: EBNA1) via nucleofection — footprint-free. (3) Culture on vitronectin in E8 medium; pick colonies at day 20–25. (4) Checkpoint 1: Karyotyping (G-banding) + whole-exome sequencing to exclude mutations. (5) Checkpoint 2: Teratoma assay in NSG mice + trilineage qPCR panel. (6) Differentiate via 7-stage protocol (Activin A → Wnt3a → FGF10 → retinoic acid → exendin-4 → nicotinamide → ALK5 inhibitor). (7) Functional assay: Glucose-stimulated insulin secretion (GSIS) — measure C-peptide release at 2.8 mM vs 16.7 mM glucose; stimulation index >2 indicates maturity. Poor answers omit karyotyping, use integrating vectors, or skip GSIS.
